sentences.text: Quetzalcoatlus northropi was one of the largest azhdarchids, a family of toothless pterosaurs characterized by unusually long and rigid necks. It rivaled in size other giants like Arambourgiania, Hatzegopteryx, and possibly Cryodrakon.

The animal possessed light, hollow bones reinforced internally by struts known as trabeculae to support its massive frame. The skull of the related species Q. lawsoni likely measured between 94 and 96 centimeters in length based on the lower jaw.
Unlike some other pterosaurs, the skull of Q. lawsoni did not exhibit cranial kinesis, making it essentially a rigid unit.
Quetzalcoatlus is one of the largest flying animals known in history.
A specific specimen of Quetzalcoatlus lawsoni shows three small oval openings on the quadrate bone that may represent puncture wounds.
When first discovered, scientists estimated the largest Quetzalcoatlus fossils came from an individual with a wingspan of about 15.9 meters.
In any case, the weight distribution in flight posture allowed at least short flights and a spectacular landing by re-balancing the weight on land.
The genus Quetzalcoatlus was described by Douglas Lawson in 1975, and the genus was named by Lawson in 1975.

The first Quetzalcoatlus fossils were discovered in 1971 by Douglas A. Lawson during his master's research. The type specimen of Quetzalcoatlus northropi consists of wing fragments found in 1971 in the Javelina Formation of Texas.
Structures initially thought to be pycnofibres were later confirmed to be conifer needles.

Recent research suggests Quetzalcoatlus likely hunted small prey on the ground, similar to storks and ground hornbills. This feeding behavior is known as the terrestrial stalking hypothesis and is common among large azhdarchids.
Quetzalcoatlus lawsoni must have been capable of taking off from limited open spaces because no nearby trees or elevations were available for launch.
Quetzalcoatlus likely used a pacing gait on the ground, moving limbs on one side simultaneously before switching to the opposite side.
Quetzalcoatlus northropi likely lived a more solitary lifestyle in a riparian habitat compared to Q. lawsoni.
Douglas Lawson suggested that Quetzalcoatlus was a scavenger similar to vultures.
In 1975, Lawson rejected a piscivorous lifestyle for Quetzalcoatlus, suggesting instead that it was a vulture-like scavenger feeding on carcasses of sauropods like Alamosaurus.
Trackways have been confidently assigned only to azhdarchids, the group that includes Quetzalcoatlus.
Quetzalcoatlus was abundant in Texas during the Lanciano age in a fauna dominated by Alamosaurus. The Alamosaurus-Quetzalcoatlus association likely represents semi-arid inland plains.
The site where the holotype was discovered is approximately 250 miles from the coastline.
The type species of the genus Quetzalcoatlus is Quetzalcoatlus northropi.
In 1984, Lev Alexandrovich Nessov erected the subfamily Azhdarchinae to contain Azhdarcho, Quetzalcoatlus, and Titanopteryx.
Quetzalcoatlus lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous. Quetzalcoatlus lived around 67 to 66 million years ago during the latest Maastrichtian.
Quetzalcoatlus lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage between 68 and 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether the species Q. lawsoni should be placed within the genus Quetzalcoatlus.
A 2010 study by Mark Witton and colleagues questioned whether Quetzalcoatlus could be validly diagnosed.
